studies.title: Sleep and body-clock measures can tell unipolar and bipolar depression apart
studies.ns_score_reason: a genuinely hard clinical problem with an unusually clean discrimination score, though the sample is modest and internal-only.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers in Paris assessed 159 patients in a current depressive episode — 43 with bipolar depression, 116 with unipolar depression — using questionnaires, wrist actigraphy and overnight polysomnography, then built a stepwise logistic model. Six sleep variables did most of the work: people with unipolar depression reported worse sleep quality and more severe insomnia and had lower actigraphic sleep efficiency, while those with bipolar depression spent longer at rest over 24 hours, were less active during their quietest and most active hours, and had more stage N2 sleep. The combined model separated the two groups with an area under the curve of 0.926.
studies.why_it_matters: Misdiagnosing bipolar depression as unipolar is one of psychiatry's costliest errors, because antidepressants alone can destabilize bipolar illness — and diagnosis currently rests on patient recall of past highs. A wearable-plus-sleep-lab signature would be an objective adjunct, if it survives external validation.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the gap this fills: people with bipolar disorder wait years for the right diagnosis because a manic episode is easy to forget or hide, and here the giveaway is how they sleep and move. Open on the everyday scene of a wrist actigraph worn for a week producing information a clinical interview missed. Call Pierre A. Geoffroy and Julia Maruani at Bichat-Claude Bernard Hospital, and ask an independent chronobiologist whether the model would hold up in an unselected outpatient population.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a health-technology or specialist psychiatry outlet on the slow migration of psychiatric diagnosis from the interview room to passive sensing — smartwatch actigraphy, keyboard dynamics, voice — and who decides when a probability score is good enough to act on.
studies.caveats: Single-center; only 20 bipolar patients had polysomnography; no external validation cohort, and the model was internally derived, so performance will almost certainly drop elsewhere; cross-sectional.

studies.title: Sleeping pills taken in pregnancy may not raise a child's risk of ADHD or autism
studies.ns_score_reason: large, well-designed national cohort with an active-comparator logic that explains away an earlier scare; the null result is the news.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Using Taiwan's national insurance and birth registries for 2009–2016, researchers restricted the cohort to children whose mothers had been diagnosed with insomnia, depression or anxiety — so that exposed and unexposed mothers were similarly unwell. Among 75,477 mother–child pairs (25,159 exposed to benzodiazepines or Z-drugs in pregnancy), prenatal exposure was not associated with later ADHD (adjusted hazard ratio 1.08, 95% CI 0.99–1.18) or autism (1.08, 0.88–1.32). Associations seen in crude analyses disappeared once maternal psychiatric severity and family factors were accounted for.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests that headline links between pregnancy sedatives and neurodevelopmental diagnoses largely reflect why the drugs were prescribed rather than the drugs themselves — a design lesson that applies well beyond this drug class.
studies.pitch_angle: The surprise is methodological and deeply human: the risk signal vanishes when you compare treated anxious mothers with untreated anxious mothers. Open on a pregnant woman told to tough out months of insomnia on the basis of a study that compared her to women who were never anxious at all. Call the Chung Shan Medical University team (Jing-Yang Huang, Hui-Ping Chang) and a perinatal pharmacoepidemiologist for the confounding-by-indication argument. Frame as evidence about prior evidence, not as prescribing advice.
studies.wider_angle: A trend piece for a general-interest or science-policy outlet on how "confounding by indication" has quietly reversed a string of drug-in-pregnancy scares, and what that pattern of retraction-by-better-design does to public trust in each new warning.
studies.caveats: Observational (cannot establish causation); residual confounding acknowledged by the authors; exposure defined from prescription claims, not verified intake; Taiwanese population may not generalize; follow-up ends by school age, so later-diagnosed cases may be missed.

studies.title: Adding exercise to school PE lessons does nothing for teenagers' mood
studies.ns_score_reason: a clean, heart-rate-monitored cluster RCT that contradicts a very popular belief; limited by size and short duration.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: In a 12-week cluster randomized trial in two Brazilian state schools, 131 adolescents (mean age 13.2, 52.7% female) either took part in structured exercise sessions inside their physical education classes — twice weekly, 20 minutes, intensity verified with heart-rate sensors — or carried on as usual. There were no group-by-time effects on depression, anxiety or stress on the DASS-21; all confidence intervals straddled zero.
studies.why_it_matters: School-based exercise is one of the most widely promoted low-cost mental health interventions for young people, and this well-monitored trial suggests that a realistic dose delivered inside the timetable is not enough to move symptom scores.
studies.pitch_angle: Play it against the familiar "exercise is as good as antidepressants" line — that evidence comes mostly from adults who are already depressed and who exercise a lot more than 40 minutes a week. Open in a PE class with heart-rate straps on, doing everything right, and getting nothing. Call Antonio Stabelini Neto at the State University of Northern Parana on the dose question, and a youth mental health trialist on whether symptom scales in a largely non-depressed sample could detect anything at all.
studies.wider_angle: An education-sector story on the gap between wellbeing policy and wellbeing evidence: schools are being asked to deliver mental health outcomes through activities that were never tested at the dose the timetable allows.
studies.caveats: Small N (131) and only two schools; 12-week intervention with no longer follow-up; participants were not selected for depressive symptoms, so floor effects are likely; self-reported outcomes.

studies.the_study: Eighty patients with moderate-to-severe depression were randomized to 20 sessions of high-frequency deep transcranial magnetic stimulation or sham over four weeks. Active stimulation reduced Hamilton depression scores significantly more than sham. Unexpectedly, patients with higher fasting triglycerides at baseline improved more — and the triglyceride–response relationship was stronger in the active arm than in sham, suggesting the blood measure modifies the treatment effect rather than merely tracking placebo response.
studies.why_it_matters: Roughly half of patients do not respond to TMS and there is no cheap way to predict who will. A routine lipid panel as a candidate response marker is an unusually practical lead — but it is one exploratory interaction in 80 people.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on the coin-flip a patient faces before committing to a month of daily clinic visits, then on the idea that a £5 blood test done for heart risk might carry information about it. Lead the surprise: a metabolic number, not a brain scan. Call the psychiatry team at the First Hospital of Hebei Medical University, and a TMS researcher outside China on biomarker replication and why lipids could plausibly bear on cortical excitability or inflammation.
studies.wider_angle: For a specialist medical or biotech outlet: the search for stratification markers in neuromodulation, and how metabolic and inflammatory phenotypes of depression are creeping into treatment-selection research after decades of one-size-fits-all trials.
studies.caveats: Small N (80); single-center; exploratory subgroup/interaction analysis with no correction or validation sample reported; abstract lacks effect sizes and follow-up beyond four weeks.

studies.title: Depression rewires how the brain handles trust from close friends
studies.ns_score_reason: preregistered, cross-task fMRI with a reversal that will surprise readers; correlational and symptom-based rather than clinical.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: In a preregistered fMRI study, 123 participants first played a reward-sharing task and then a Trust Game with a close friend, a stranger and a computer. People with more depressive symptoms actually invested *more* in their friend relative to the computer. Striatal sensitivity to shared reward predicted temporoparietal junction responses when trust was reciprocated — but the direction of that link flipped in participants who had both higher depressive symptoms and closer relationships.
studies.why_it_matters: It shifts the story about depression and relationships from simple social withdrawal to something stranger: the machinery for interpreting a friend's goodwill appears to be recalibrated, not switched off.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the counterintuitive behavior — depressed participants trusted their friends more with real money, while their brains processed the payback differently. Open on the moment in the scanner when a friend sends money back. Call David V. Smith's lab at Temple University; ask what "closeness calibrates the signal" would look like in daily life, and be explicit that these are symptom scores in a community sample, not diagnosed patients.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on the neuroscience of friendship for a psychology or general-interest outlet — how the brain treats a known person differently from a stranger or an algorithm, and what happens to that distinction in mood disorders, autism and loneliness.
studies.caveats: Observational and cross-sectional; depressive symptoms self-reported in a non-clinical sample; N=123 is decent for fMRI but small for three-way interactions; updated from a bioRxiv preprint.

studies.title: Distrusting doctors a little makes Black adults more likely to seek mental health help — distrusting them a lot does not
studies.ns_score_reason: a non-linear result that undercuts the standard "mistrust equals avoidance" framing, in a large survey; cross-sectional and hypothetical-willingness outcome.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: An online cross-sectional survey of 1042 Black adults in the US measured group-based medical mistrust, willingness to seek help and depressive symptoms (PHQ-9). Compared with the lowest-mistrust quartile, those in the middle quartiles were far more willing to seek help from a mental health professional (odds ratios 3.7 and 5.0), while the highest-mistrust quartile was less willing than the middle groups. Adding depressive symptoms to the model reduced willingness to seek professional help by an average of 25.7%.
studies.why_it_matters: Mistrust is usually treated as a simple barrier to care; here the relationship is curved, and depression itself — the very thing treatment would address — independently dampens help-seeking.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is the inverted-U: a healthy skepticism about institutions goes with *more* willingness to look for help, and only at the extreme does it become avoidance. Open on someone vetting a therapist carefully rather than refusing one. Call Aderonke Bamgbose Pederson at Massachusetts General Brigham. Note her disclosed industry compensation, and keep the framing to willingness, not actual treatment uptake.
studies.wider_angle: A public-health piece for a policy or general-interest outlet on why anti-stigma campaigns keep underperforming: the people least likely to seek help may be held back by the symptoms themselves — anergia, hopelessness, self-blame — rather than by beliefs a campaign can change.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional (cannot establish causation); self-reported, hypothetical willingness rather than service use; online convenience sample; author has received payments from Otsuka, Apple Inc. and Quality Interactions.

studies.ns_score_reason: a large, nine-year, transdiagnostic dataset that says something concrete and relatable about personality and chronicity; still correlational.

studies.the_study: Drawing on 1800 participants at the nine-year follow-up of the Netherlands Study of Depression and Anxiety, researchers mapped interpersonal problems onto the four quadrants of the interpersonal circumplex and compared people with current, past and no lifetime anxiety or depression. Those currently diagnosed reported more general interpersonal distress and a more submissive style than the other two groups. A specifically "cold-submissive" style — distant and unassertive — was associated with greater comorbidity and chronicity, even after adjusting for demographics.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests a measurable relational signature of long-running, overlapping anxiety and depression, and an obvious therapeutic target; whether the style drives chronicity or is shaped by it remains open.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the finding that the current-diagnosis group and the recovered group differ in how they relate to other people — distance and deference look like features of being unwell now, not just of having been unwell. Open on a patient who has recovered on paper but still cannot ask a colleague for anything. Call the Groningen team (Jill Peters, Peter J. de Jong) and ask what distinguishes cause from consequence in nine-year data.
studies.wider_angle: A longer read for a psychology or features desk on the interpersonal circumplex — a 1950s idea now being used to predict who gets chronically ill and who responds to therapy — and on the shift from symptom-counting to relationship-mapping in psychiatric assessment.
studies.caveats: Observational cohort; interpersonal style measured only at follow-up, so temporal ordering is unclear; self-reported IIP; Dutch cohort with high baseline psychopathology may not generalize.

studies.ns_score_reason: a clean dissociation over 11 years of follow-up, in a group rarely studied at this depth; modest N and self-reported outcomes.

studies.the_study: Using longitudinal data from 592 Black Americans in the Milwaukee sample of the Midlife in the United States study (2005–06 to 2016–17), researchers tested six dimensions of social connectedness against psychological distress and depression, with loneliness and frequency of social contact as competing mediators. Loneliness predicted both distress and depression (β=1.76; aOR=2.14); social isolation, measured as contact frequency, predicted neither. Family support had the strongest total protective effect — mostly channelled through reduced loneliness (aOR 0.54), plus a direct effect on depression (aOR 0.30).
studies.why_it_matters: For midlife Black Americans at least, the mental health payoff comes from feeling connected rather than from the count of interactions, and family is where most of that feeling is generated.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the split: two people with identical diaries, one lonely and one not, and only the lonely one heading for depression a decade later. Open on the family-support finding, which does the heavy lifting and is culturally specific in a way most loneliness research ignores. Call Yusuf Ransome at the Yale School of Public Health and ask why friend support did not do the same work.
studies.wider_angle: For a general-interest or health-policy outlet: the "loneliness epidemic" is being fought with interventions that add contact — apps, groups, befriending calls — when the data point to the perceived quality of existing family bonds. A story about what an evidence-led loneliness policy would actually fund.
studies.caveats: Observational (cannot establish causation); N=592 from a single city sample; depression assessed by a brief 7-item self-report measure; social isolation operationalized only as contact frequency.

studies.ns_score_reason: very large linked-records cohort with a higher-than-textbook estimate and an odd socioeconomic twist; algorithmic case definition limits precision.

studies.the_study: Researchers applied an algorithm to healthcare utilization records for 164,767 women who gave birth in the Milan metropolitan area between 2017 and 2023, and cross-checked against Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale screening. Some 16% had perinatal depression-related events, and 23.6% of screened mothers scored EPDS ≥8. The strongest risk factor by far was psychological distress in the 12 months before pregnancy (OR 8.1), followed by age over 40, migrant background, being unmarried and first-time motherhood. Counter to expectation, lower education and employment appeared modestly protective.
studies.why_it_matters: The conventional figure for perinatal depression is 10–15%; a routine-records approach across an entire metropolitan population lands higher, and points to the year *before* conception as the key prediction window.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the pre-pregnancy signal: the single best predictor of perinatal depression showed up in the records before the woman was pregnant, with an eightfold odds ratio. Open on the routine contacts — a GP visit, a prescription — that already contain the warning. Call Antonio Giampiero Russo's epidemiology unit at ATS Milano, and ask about the inverted education finding, which may be a care-access artefact rather than protection.
studies.wider_angle: A data-journalism piece for a health or technology outlet on "phenotyping from admin data": whole populations diagnosed retrospectively by algorithm from prescriptions and appointments, what it reveals, and what it gets wrong when access to care varies by class and citizenship.
studies.caveats: Observational; cases defined by an unvalidated utilization algorithm, so the 16% mixes true incidence with care-seeking; EPDS figures come only from the screened subgroup; single region in Italy.

studies.ns_score_reason: large sample and a nicely contrarian detail, but it sits inside a scale-mapping paper and is cross-sectional.

studies.the_study: In a population-based US sample of 1794 adults enriched for high perceived stress and trauma exposure, researchers ran network analyses on the Mount Sinai Resilience Scale alongside measures of depression, anxiety, PTSD and wellbeing. Staying hopeful, deliberately facing feared situations and engaging in meaningful activities were consistently linked to fewer symptoms across all three disorders. Forgiveness, by contrast, was *positively* associated with PTSD symptoms.
studies.why_it_matters: The resilience literature tends to treat all positive-sounding traits as interchangeably protective; this suggests they are not, and that "approach" behaviors matter more than conciliatory ones.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the forgiveness anomaly — the most culturally endorsed healing prescription is the one item swimming against the tide. Open on a survivor being urged to forgive. Call Robert H. Pietrzak at Yale, who can speak to whether forgiveness here reflects coping effort in people who are still suffering, rather than a cause of suffering. Note the extensive Mount Sinai intellectual-property disclosures on the paper.
studies.wider_angle: A cultural-science feature for a general-interest outlet on forgiveness as therapy — its religious roots, its adoption by clinical psychology, and the thin evidence that telling trauma survivors to forgive helps them.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional (cannot establish causation); all self-report; sample enriched for stress and trauma, so not representative; co-authors hold patents and licensing interests in resilience and depression products (Janssen, Click Therapeutics), disclosed in the paper.

studies.title: Women in ongoing depression treatment conceive less often during fertility care
studies.ns_score_reason: striking national-scale numbers on a question patients actually ask, but confounding by indication is so severe that the authors themselves warn against interpretation.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: From 601,664 South Korean women aged 20–45 receiving infertility care between 2017 and 2023, researchers built a cohort of 8734 women without depression and 4367 with it, split by treatment timing. Compared with controls, women whose antidepressant treatment was in the past had a slightly *higher* rate of first recorded pregnancy (adjusted sHR 1.10), while those on ongoing treatment (0.53) or newly started treatment (0.31) had markedly lower rates. Among treated women, greater prescription coverage went with a higher hazard of pregnancy — a finding the authors explicitly say should not be read as adherence improving fertility.
studies.why_it_matters: Not much is settled yet, but the timing pattern is the interesting part: recovered depression looks unremarkable for conception, whereas active illness or newly started treatment does not — and untangling drug from illness will need a far better design.
studies.pitch_angle: Frame it around the question fertility patients put to clinicians constantly — should I come off my antidepressant? — and the honest answer this study gives, which is that claims data cannot tell drug from disease. Open on a woman weighing an IVF cycle against a prescription. Call the CHA University authors (Wonsuk Shin, Sra Jung) and ask what design would settle it; pair with a reproductive psychiatrist. Do not imply any prescribing action.
studies.wider_angle: For a specialist medicine or women's health outlet: the persistent evidence vacuum around psychiatric medication and reproduction, and why pregnancy and fertility populations remain systematically excluded from the trials that would answer their questions.
studies.caveats: Retrospective claims analysis; observational (cannot establish causation); confounding by indication, exposure timing and reverse causation all flagged by the authors; pregnancy identified from claims, so early losses and non-clinical conceptions may be missed; South Korean insurance population.

studies.title: People whose brains respond least to reward gain most from a single mood-training session
studies.ns_score_reason: a neat randomized test of who benefits from a brief intervention, undermined by small N, attrition and a null primary effect.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Ninety-two US college students (mean age 19.4) were randomized to a single session of Brief Promoting Positive Emotions training or a study-skills comparison, then completed a monetary incentive delay task while EEG recorded the reward positivity (RewP) — a brain response to winning. The training did not change RewP. But RewP predicted who benefited: in the training group, a blunted reward response was associated with *lower* perceived stress a month later, whereas in the comparison group blunted RewP went with rising stress. There were no effects on depression or social anxiety symptoms.
studies.why_it_matters: Blunted reward response is usually read as a straight risk marker; here it identifies exactly the people a brief positive-emotion training helps, which is the logic personalized psychological care has been promising for years.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the inversion — the brain signal that flags vulnerability also flags who responds to a 60-minute intervention. Open on two students with the same flat EEG response, one of whom sat through the training. Call Autumn Kujawa's lab at Vanderbilt and press on the null main effect and the honest question of whether an EEG cap will ever be worth it for triaging a one-session program.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a psychology or higher-education outlet on the campus mental health triage problem: thousands of students, no capacity for therapy for all, and a growing effort to work out in advance who needs what — with EEG, apps and stepped care all competing.
studies.caveats: Small N (92, dropping to 66 at follow-up); primary intervention effect on RewP was null, so this is a moderation finding; single site; non-clinical student sample; self-reported outcomes; one-month follow-up.

studies.the_study: Researchers assessed 407 patients within the first week after acute stroke, using the short German Self-Compassion Scale and the PHQ-9. Self-compassion split into two factors: compassionate and uncompassionate self-responding. In structural equation models adjusting for sociodemographic and clinical risk factors, uncompassionate self-responding — self-judgment, isolation, over-identification with distress — added the most explanatory power for depressive symptoms (ΔR²=0.057), more than the compassionate side.
studies.why_it_matters: Post-stroke depression affects around a third of survivors and is poorly predicted by lesion or severity measures; how patients speak to themselves in the acute ward may be a tractable additional signal, pending longitudinal work.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the asymmetry: it is not the absence of self-kindness that matters most but the presence of self-attack, measured within days of the stroke. Open on a patient in an acute ward blaming themselves for a weak hand. Call Luisa Beerbaum and Ulrike Dinger in Düsseldorf and ask whether the acute-phase measure predicts depression months later — the study cannot say yet.
studies.wider_angle: A rehabilitation-medicine story for a health or specialist outlet on the neglected psychological side of stroke units: why teams measure grip strength and swallow reflexes daily but almost never how a patient is talking to themselves.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional (cannot establish causation, and depressed mood may drive self-judgment rather than the reverse); single-center; self-report measures administered to acutely ill patients; the compassionate-self-responding subscale had weak reliability (ω=0.63).

studies.the_study: Left Write Hook is a peer-led, survivor-designed program combining trauma-focused expressive writing with non-contact, trauma-informed boxing. Seventeen women and gender-diverse survivors of childhood sexual abuse completed eight weekly two-hour sessions. From pre- to post-program, self-reported PTSD, complex PTSD, depression, anxiety and stress all fell significantly, alongside reductions in maladaptive post-traumatic cognitions and trauma memory fragmentation, and increases in emotional wellbeing and vigorous physical activity.
studies.why_it_matters: It is a proof of concept for a delivery model that does not require a clinical psychologist per participant — and one of the few trauma interventions to target the body and the narrative simultaneously.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the pairing that sounds implausible and the specific finding that trauma memories became less fragmented — a cognitive change, produced by a program run by survivors in a boxing gym. Open on a participant hitting pads after writing about her childhood. Call Caitlin Hitchcock at the University of Melbourne and program originator Donna Lyon; be straight that 17 people with no control group cannot show the boxing did it.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a general-interest or arts-and-culture outlet on peer-designed mental health care — survivors building the intervention they wanted and then having to prove it to a clinical research system built around expert-led manuals.
studies.caveats: Small N (17); no control group; self-reported outcomes; single site; self-selected, motivated participants; no follow-up beyond end of program; expectancy effects likely in a highly engaging group intervention.

studies.title: Half of trafficking survivors have depression, global review finds
studies.ns_score_reason: the first pooled global quantification of a hidden burden, but the heterogeneity is so extreme that the numbers are planning aids, not estimates.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run

studies.the_study: A preregistered systematic review and meta-analysis of 18 quantitative studies (2000–2025) of survivors of trafficking for sexual exploitation pooled prevalence at 44.0% for PTSD, 50.5% for depression, 52.3% for anxiety and 19.1% for suicide attempts. Heterogeneity was extreme (I² 96.9–98.9%), with a prediction interval for PTSD spanning 7.0–89.1%. Region explained variation only for depression. Just two studies reported usable data on service use; none measured the structural determinants of survivors' access to care.
studies.why_it_matters: It puts a first global number on a psychiatric burden that has been asserted rather than measured — and documents that the literature has almost nothing to say about whether survivors ever reach treatment.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the second finding, which is the more damning one: 18 studies, tens of thousands of survivors, and two papers that recorded whether anyone got help. Open on the prediction interval — 7% to 89% for PTSD — as a picture of how little we know. Call Ayşe Yıldız Karaahmet and Fatma İlknur Uzun at Biruni University, and a trafficking-services clinician for ground truth.
studies.wider_angle: An investigative or global-health feature on why survivor mental health data is so poor: samples of convenience drawn from shelters and prosecutions, no follow-up after repatriation, and research funding that stops where the legal case does.
studies.caveats: Extreme between-study heterogeneity means pooled figures should not be read as population prevalence; only 18 studies, four of them for suicide attempts; samples drawn largely from service-contact populations, so likely biased toward the most severely affected; secondary analysis of published data.

studies.the_study: Ninety patients at two specialist psychosocial centers for refugees in Germany completed PTSD and depression questionnaires at the start of treatment, midway and at the end of multidisciplinary trauma- and migration-focused care. studies.the_study: Using NHANES data on 30,244 US adults, researchers compared PHQ-9-defined depressive symptoms against the American Heart Association's cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) staging. Sixteen per cent of adults had advanced CKM (stages 3–4) and 8% had depressive symptoms. Fully adjusted models found depressive symptoms associated with advanced CKM in both sexes, more strongly in women (OR 2.24) than men (OR 1.75), with a formal interaction favoring women; the association was much weaker in people aged 65 and over than in those aged 30–49.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests the mind–body link in cardiometabolic disease is concentrated in younger and middle-aged women — a group whose cardiovascular risk is routinely underestimated.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the age finding, which is the odd one: the depression–organ damage association is strongest in people in their 30s and 40s and fades after 65, the opposite of what an accumulation model predicts. Open on a 40-year-old woman screened for depression but not for kidney function. Call Leonard E. Egede's group, and be explicit that a cross-sectional survey cannot say which came first.
studies.wider_angle: For a specialist cardiology or general health outlet: the arrival of "CKM syndrome" as a unified staging system, and the argument over whether depression belongs in the model as a risk factor, a consequence, or a shared-inflammation cousin.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional (cannot establish causation, and reverse causation is entirely plausible); depressive symptoms by self-report questionnaire, not diagnosis; multiple interaction tests; US survey population.

studies.title: Chronic pelvic pain leaves a distinct mark on body image
studies.ns_score_reason: first pooled estimate for a very common and under-researched condition, with a usable moderate effect size; input studies are mostly cross-sectional and weak.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 22 studies (N=7609) of endometriosis and other chronic pelvic pain conditions, including vulvodynia, found body image concerns significantly worse than in healthy controls (g=0.50, 95% CI 0.30–0.69). Body image disturbance was linked to anxiety, depression, loneliness, sexual dysfunction and distress across conditions. The authors identify "body functionality" — what the body can do rather than how it looks — as a possible mediator between pain symptoms and body image, and a candidate intervention target.
studies.why_it_matters: Endometriosis affects roughly one in ten women of reproductive age, and this quantifies a psychological cost that rarely features in the diagnostic or treatment conversation.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the reframing: body image research is dominated by appearance, and here the thing that seems to matter is a body that hurts and cannot be relied on. Open on someone with endometriosis describing her body as an adversary. Call Kerry A. Sherman at Macquarie University on the body-functionality construct and whether it is trainable.
studies.wider_angle: A women's health feature — for a general-interest or health outlet — on the average eight-year diagnostic delay in endometriosis and what years of being disbelieved does to a person's relationship with her own body, with the depression and loneliness associations as the evidence spine.
studies.caveats: Secondary analysis; most included studies cross-sectional with limited theoretical grounding and variable body image measures; heterogeneous conditions pooled; publication bias not described in the abstract; samples largely from high-income clinical settings.

studies.title: Patients lost weight over a year on a new antipsychotic
studies.ns_score_reason: reverses the expected metabolic direction for an antipsychotic, but open-label, industry-run, 62% dropout, and only tangentially about depression.
studies.media_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: In a one-year open-label Phase 3 study, 602 adult outpatients with stable schizophrenia took lumateperone 42 mg daily for 368 days; 229 (38%) completed. The most common adverse event was weight *decreased* (10.1%). Total and LDL cholesterol, triglycerides and prolactin all improved significantly, as did weight, BMI and waist circumference, with no notable extrapyramidal signal. Symptom scores improved modestly, including on the Calgary Depression Scale for Schizophrenia (mean change −0.6, effect size −0.21).
studies.why_it_matters: Metabolic harm is the main reason people stop taking antipsychotics and a major driver of their shortened life expectancy, so a drug that moves those numbers the other way is worth watching — but an uncontrolled study with 62% attrition cannot establish it.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the reversal of the most notorious side effect in psychiatry, then immediately with the reason for caution: no comparator, and nearly two-thirds of patients left. Open on the weight-gain trade-off patients are routinely asked to accept. Call Christoph U. Correll — while noting his extensive industry disclosures — and an independent psychopharmacologist on what dropout does to metabolic averages. Funder: Intra-Cellular Therapies, a Johnson & Johnson company.
studies.wider_angle: For a specialist pharma or health-business outlet: how "metabolically clean" has become the competitive axis in antipsychotic development, and whether open-label extension studies can ever settle such claims.
studies.caveats: Open-label with no control group; 62% did not complete, so completer-biased metabolic results are likely; industry-funded and industry-authored (Intra-Cellular Therapies / Johnson & Johnson); depression outcome was a small secondary effect in people with schizophrenia, not a depression population.

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**
- **Felt experience beats counted exposure.** "It is loneliness, not how often you see people, that predicts depression" (PMID 42623964) lands squarely on the thread opened last month by "Prolonged childhood loneliness roughly triples the odds of a first psychotic episode" (PMID 42636467), where subjective loneliness, not premorbid isolation, carried the risk — and by the subjective-versus-administrative finding in "Students who wrongly believe they're first-generation are the hungriest" (PMID 42634162). Three runs of data now say the same thing: the self-report question outperforms the objective proxy.
- **Confounding by indication keeps dissolving risk signals.** "Sleeping pills taken in pregnancy may not raise a child's risk of ADHD or autism" (PMID 42744942) and "Women in ongoing depression treatment conceive less often during fertility care" (PMID 42735740) are the same argument the GLP-1 Bradford Hill review made last month (PMID 42624955), and that the parental-drinking meta-analysis made when adjusted effects attenuated (PMID 42665302). The active-comparator design in the Taiwanese cohort is the cleanest version of it yet.
- **Depression as a multiplier of somatic burden.** "Depression's link to advanced heart, kidney and metabolic disease is stronger in women" (PMID 42747918) extends the fibromyalgia interaction from the previous digest, where depression and central sensitization compounded each other (PMID 42660390). Both point to depression as a co-traveling amplifier rather than a substitute explanation for physical illness.
- **Popular interventions underperforming.** "Adding exercise to school PE lessons does nothing for teenagers' mood" (PMID 42752288) and "Forgiveness goes with worse, not better, post-traumatic symptoms" (PMID 42664566) continue the deflationary run of the last digest — null VR support groups (PMID 42661554), null transfer from perinatal prevention to parenting warmth (PMID 42593980), no independent role for resilience or social support in refugees (PMID 42642861).

**Advances**
- **Treatment-matching markers are multiplying.** Last month's standout moderator finding was the ANTOP six-year analysis, where baseline depression severity determined which anorexia therapy worked (PMID 42611819), alongside an externally validated 37-item outcome predictor (PMID 42640866). This month adds two physiological candidates: "Blood fat levels predict who responds to magnetic brain stimulation for depression" (PMID 42720531) and "People whose brains respond least to reward gain most from a single mood-training session" (PMID 42700813). The stratification question has moved from questionnaires to blood panels and EEG.
- **Objective diagnostic markers, better result.** "Sleep and body-clock measures can tell unipolar and bipolar depression apart" (PMID 42751051) reaches an AUC of 0.926 from actigraphy and polysomnography, which is a sharp contrast to the two biomarker stories in the previous digest — the reversed retinal thickness direction (PMID 42637150) and the failure to decode rumination from EEG in more than 10 of 24 people (PMID 42648371). Passive sensing of *state and diagnosis* looks more tractable than passive sensing of *momentary cognition*.

**Counterpoints**
- **Low-tech and embodied versus immersive.** Avatar-based VR support groups lost to a room with chairs last month (PMID 42661554); this month "Boxing and expressive writing improve mental health in survivors of childhood sexual abuse" (PMID 42752360) reports pre-post gains from a peer-led, physical, survivor-designed program — uncontrolled, but pointing in the opposite technological direction.
- **A protective-factor null that cuts the other way.** Where the refugee resilience study found no independent buffering (PMID 42642861), "Refugees keep their therapy gains even when asylum decisions change" (PMID 42703887) finds no independent *harm* from legal limbo — a null that supports service provision rather than undercutting it.

**New themes**
- **Relationship-mapping as psychiatric measurement.** "A cold, deferential social style marks out the most stubborn depression" (PMID 42731108) and "Depression rewires how the brain handles trust from close friends" (PMID 42702279) have no clear antecedent in the previous digest; together with the loneliness paper they suggest a shift from symptom counting to characterizing how depressed people actually transact with others.
- **Reproductive and women's mental health as a cluster.** Five studies this month (PMIDs 42744942, 42745087, 42735740, 42752993, 42600312) with nothing comparable last month. See below.
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Five studies in this batch address depression in women's reproductive lives, and every one of them answers the question with registry algorithms, claims data or pooled reviews because no trial exists: sleeping pills in pregnancy cleared by an active-comparator national cohort (PMID 42744942), one in six new mothers flagged by an unvalidated utilization algorithm across metropolitan Milan (PMID 42745087), antidepressant timing and conception inferred from South Korean insurance claims with the authors themselves warning against interpretation (PMID 42735740), trafficking survivors' 50.5% pooled depression prevalence with a PTSD prediction interval of 7–89% (PMID 42752993), and the first pooled estimate of body image disturbance in endometriosis and chronic pelvic pain (PMID 42600312). "Depression's link to advanced heart, kidney and metabolic disease is stronger in women" (PMID 42747918) adds a sex-specific physical-health signal drawn, again, from a cross-sectional survey.

**Why pitch this now:** These are precisely the decisions women are asked to make in real time — stay on the antidepressant through IVF, tough out insomnia in the third trimester — and the honest state of the evidence is that the answers are being reverse-engineered from prescription and billing records because the relevant populations are routinely excluded from trials.

**Angle:** A reported feature on what it looks like when a whole field of clinical questions is answered by administrative data: what registry epidemiology can genuinely settle (the pregnancy-sedative scare, the pre-conception prediction window), what it cannot (drug versus disease in fertility care), and who pays for the gap. Written for a general reader who has been handed a risk statistic in a consulting room and wants to know where it came from.

**Potential headlines:**
- The evidence on depression and pregnancy is being assembled from insurance claims
- A pregnancy drug scare that disappeared when researchers found a fairer comparison group
- Women are deciding about antidepressants on evidence no trial has ever produced

**Potential outlets:**
- **New Scientist Features** — the batch supports a long read on method and evidence quality rather than a single result, and the pregnancy-sedative reversal gives it a concrete narrative spine.
- **STAT** — the prescribing, exclusion-from-trials and reproductive-psychiatry strands are core to their pharma and clinical-practice coverage.
- **The Guardian science and health desk** — has run sustained coverage of the endometriosis diagnostic delay and the women's health evidence gap, which this pitch quantifies.
- **Undark** — built for scrutiny of research infrastructure: algorithmic case definitions, confounding by indication, and the populations research design leaves out.

# Fact-Check Report: New Scientist Story Ideas — Depression — September 2026
**Checked:** 2026-09-18 | **Studies reviewed:** 19
**Publication:** New Scientist | **Section:** New Scientist Mind

# Fact-Check Report — New Scientist Mind digest, run date 2026-09-18

---

### Study 1: Sleep and body-clock measures can tell unipolar and bipolar depression apart
**PMID:** 42751051 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

All numbers check out: 159 patients (43 BDD, 116 UDD), AUC 0.926, the six retained variables, and the direction of each sleep difference all match the abstract, as do the PSG subsample figure (20 BDD) flagged in Caveats.

**Issue A. Headline states a capability the study has not demonstrated** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Sleep and body-clock measures can tell unipolar and bipolar depression apart"
- **Abstract says:** "Integrating subjective, actigraphic, and polysomnographic markers provides a promising, noninvasive approach to differentiate UDD from BDD."
- **Problem:** The 0.926 AUC comes from a backward stepwise model derived and evaluated in the same 159 patients, with no validation cohort. "Can tell apart" reads as an established capability; the authors claim only promise. The body text and Caveats are appropriately hedged, so only the headline is out of step.
- **Suggested fix:** "Sleep and body-clock measures show promise for telling unipolar and bipolar depression apart"

**Issue B. NS fit score rests on an unvalidated, internally derived model** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**NS fit:** 7/10 — a genuinely hard clinical problem with an unusually clean discrimination score, though the sample is modest and internal-only."
- **Abstract says:** Model derived by backward stepwise logistic regression in the same sample; explains 49.4% of variance; no external validation reported.
- **Problem:** A 7 implies this is close to pitch-ready. Stepwise selection plus in-sample AUC in 43 cases versus 116 controls, with PSG available for fewer than half the bipolar group, is exactly the setup that produces optimistic discrimination figures. The digest names this, then scores as if it did not matter.
- **Suggested fix:** Score 6/10 and note explicitly that the AUC is an in-sample estimate.

---

### Study 2: Sleeping pills taken in pregnancy may not raise a child's risk of ADHD or autism
**PMID:** 42744942 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N (75,477 pairs; 25,159 exposed), registry years (2009–2016), the restricted-cohort design, and both adjusted hazard ratios with CIs are reproduced correctly.

**Issue A. "Disappeared" overstates "attenuated"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Associations seen in crude analyses disappeared once maternal psychiatric severity and family factors were accounted for."
- **Abstract says:** "Associations observed in crude analyses were attenuated after adjusting for maternal psychiatric severity and familial factors."
- **Problem:** The adjusted ADHD estimate is 1.08 with an upper CI bound of 1.18 — compatible with an 18% relative increase. The signal shrank and lost significance; it did not vanish. "Disappeared" is the word a sceptical editor will check first.
- **Suggested fix:** "Associations seen in crude analyses were substantially attenuated once maternal psychiatric severity and family factors were accounted for, leaving estimates that no longer reached significance."

**Issue B. Affiliation attributed to the wrong institution** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Call the Chung Shan Medical University team (Jing-Yang Huang, Hui-Ping Chang)"
- **Abstract says:** Huang JY — Chung Shan Medical University; Chang HP — "Department of Nursing, Asia University, Taichung. csha615@asia.edu.tw."
- **Problem:** The corresponding author, Chang, is at Asia University, not Chung Shan. Small, but it is the contact detail a writer would act on.
- **Suggested fix:** "Call the Taichung team — Jing-Yang Huang at Chung Shan Medical University and corresponding author Hui-Ping Chang at Asia University"

**Issue C. Follow-up window not supported by the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "follow-up ends by school age, so later-diagnosed cases may be missed"
- **Abstract says:** Registry data 2009–2016; no follow-up end date or mean follow-up duration is reported.
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only. The abstract gives incidence in person-months but never states how long children were tracked.
- **Suggested fix:** "Follow-up duration is not stated in the abstract; later-diagnosed cases may be missed."

---

### Study 3: Adding exercise to school PE lessons does nothing for teenagers' mood
**PMID:** 42752288 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=131, 52.7% female, age 13.2 ± 0.90, two public schools in Brazil, 12 weeks, twice weekly, 20 minutes, heart-rate monitoring and the three null DASS-21 interaction effects are all accurate, and "all confidence intervals straddled zero" is correct for all three outcomes.

**Issue A. Headline converts an underpowered null into a definitive absence of effect** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Adding exercise to school PE lessons does nothing for teenagers' mood"
- **Abstract says:** "No significant group × time interaction effects were observed for depression (interaction effect: 0.71; 95% CI -0.98 to 2.40; p = 0.412)... The intervention was not effective in improving adolescents' mental health indicators."
- **Problem:** The depression CI runs from -0.98 to 2.40 — the trial cannot exclude a clinically meaningful benefit or harm in either direction. With 131 students in two schools, unselected for symptoms, "does nothing" is a claim the data do not support; "did not improve" is. The Caveats correctly flag floor effects, so the headline contradicts the digest's own limitation.
- **Suggested fix:** "Adding exercise to school PE lessons failed to improve teenagers' mood in a monitored trial"

**Issue B. "Failed replication" novelty label is not what the abstract describes** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**Novelty:** Failed replication"
- **Abstract says:** Title: "School-based physical exercise intervention for adolescents' mental health: An adaptation of the 'ActTeens Program' cluster RCT."
- **Problem:** This is a locally adapted intervention tested in a new population, not an attempt to reproduce a specific prior positive result. Labelling it a failed replication implies a direct head-to-head with an earlier finding that the abstract does not describe.
- **Suggested fix:** "**Novelty:** Null result that challenges a popular assumption"

---

### Study 4: Blood fat levels predict who responds to magnetic brain stimulation for depression
**PMID:** 42720531 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=80 (40/40), 20 sessions over four weeks, HAMD-17 primary outcome, greater reduction with active than sham, higher baseline triglycerides associated with greater improvement, and a stronger TG–response relationship in the active arm are all faithful to the abstract. The Caveat that the abstract reports no effect sizes is correct and well made.

**Issue A. "Single-center" not supported by the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Caveats: Small N (80); single-center"
- **Abstract says:** Authors are affiliated with The First Hospital of Hebei Medical University (five authors) and Xuzhou Medical University Affiliated Peace Hospital (one author, Internal Medicine).
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only. The abstract never states the number of recruiting sites.
- **Suggested fix:** "Recruitment site(s) not stated in the abstract; authorship is concentrated at a single hospital."

**Issue B. "New mechanism" label overstates what was tested** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**Novelty:** New mechanism"
- **Abstract says:** "could serve as a potential exploratory biomarker for individualized dTMS treatment strategies."
- **Problem:** No mechanism was investigated — this is a candidate predictive biomarker and an interaction term. The digest's own pitch angle asks a TMS researcher to speculate about plausible mechanisms, which confirms none is in the paper.
- **Suggested fix:** "**Novelty:** Candidate predictive biomarker (exploratory)"

---

### Study 5: Depression rewires how the brain handles trust from close friends
**PMID:** 42702279 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=123, preregistration, the two tasks, the three partner types, the counterintuitive investment behavior, the striatal SRS → TPJ association and its reversal under high depression plus high closeness are all accurately reported, and the Caveats correctly flag the bioRxiv update and the non-clinical sample.

**Issue A. Causal headline for a correlational, symptom-based study** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Depression rewires how the brain handles trust from close friends"
- **Abstract says:** "depression alters how striatal SRS relates to regional activity, potentially disrupting how individuals interpret and respond to close others" — in a cross-sectional design where "Depressive symptoms and perceived closeness were assessed via self-report."
- **Problem:** "Rewires" asserts a causal, structural change produced by depression. What was observed is that self-reported symptom severity moderated a correlation between two brain measures in a community sample — no diagnosed patients, no longitudinal data, no intervention. The digest's pitch angle correctly tells the writer to be explicit about this, which the headline then undoes.
- **Suggested fix:** "Depressive symptoms go with a different brain response to trust from close friends"

---

### Study 6: Distrusting doctors a little makes Black adults more likely to seek mental health help — distrusting them a lot does not
**PMID:** 42749881 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=1042, the three instruments, the ordinal logistic models, ORs of 3.73 and 5.02 for quartiles 2 and 3, and the 25.7% figure are all accurate. The body sentence "the highest-mistrust quartile was less willing than the middle groups" is a correct reading of the abstract. Industry compensation is disclosed in Caveats as required.

**Issue A. Headline misstates the highest-mistrust result and adds causal language** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Distrusting doctors a little makes Black adults more likely to seek mental health help — distrusting them a lot does not"
- **Abstract says:** "Black adults at the highest level of mistrust were less likely to seek help from a mental health professional than quartiles 2 and 3 (Quartile 4 OR = 2.38; 95%CI = 1.75, 3.25; p < 0.001)"
- **Problem:** Two errors. First, the Q4 odds ratio of 2.38 is relative to the *lowest*-mistrust quartile — so the highest-mistrust group was still markedly *more* willing to seek help than the least mistrustful group, just less so than the middle quartiles. "Distrusting them a lot does not" reverses this. Second, "makes" is causal language for a cross-sectional survey of hypothetical willingness.
- **Suggested fix:** "Moderate mistrust of doctors goes with more willingness to seek mental health help among Black adults — and the very highest mistrust with less than that"

**Issue B. "Dampens help-seeking" reads a causal, behavioural effect into a model-fit statistic** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "depression itself — the very thing treatment would address — independently dampens help-seeking"
- **Abstract says:** "The inclusion of depressive symptoms in the model resulted in a 25.7% average decrease in willingness to seek help from a mental health professional. Depressive symptoms may have an impact on the effect of medical mistrust..."
- **Problem:** The 25.7% is a change in modelled willingness on adding a covariate, in cross-sectional data, with a hypothetical-willingness outcome. "Independently dampens help-seeking" implies a demonstrated causal effect on real behaviour. The pitch angle rightly says "keep the framing to willingness, not actual treatment uptake" — the Why it matters line does not.
- **Suggested fix:** "depressive symptoms are associated with lower reported willingness to seek professional help, independent of mistrust"

---

### Study 7: A cold, deferential social style marks out the most stubborn depression
**PMID:** 42731108 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=1800 at the NESDA nine-year follow-up, the Structural Summary Method and circumplex quadrants, the current-diagnosis group's higher distress and more submissive style, and the cold-submissive association with comorbidity and chronicity after demographic adjustment are all correct. The Caveat that interpersonal style was measured only at follow-up matches the design.

**Issue A. Headline drops the anxiety half of a transdiagnostic finding** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "A cold, deferential social style marks out the most stubborn depression"
- **Abstract says:** "a cold-submissive style was associated with greater comorbidity and chronicity" of "anxiety and/or depression"; the paper is explicitly framed as "longitudinal, transdiagnostic data."
- **Problem:** The chronicity and comorbidity variables span anxiety and depressive disorders together — indeed, comorbidity is part of the outcome. Attaching the finding to depression alone narrows it inaccurately, and the body text ("overlapping anxiety and depression") is more faithful than the headline.
- **Suggested fix:** "A cold, deferential social style marks out the most stubborn anxiety and depression"

**Issue B. "New mechanism" label not supported** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**Novelty:** New mechanism"
- **Abstract says:** "Interpersonal functioning has a complex, bidirectional relationship with mental disorders"; results are cross-sectional associations of IIP-derived style with diagnostic status.
- **Problem:** Nothing mechanistic was tested, and the authors flag bidirectionality. The digest's own Why it matters concedes "whether the style drives chronicity or is shaped by it remains open."
- **Suggested fix:** "**Novelty:** New association / clinical marker"

---

### Study 8: It is loneliness, not how often you see people, that predicts depression
**PMID:** 42623964 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=592, MIDUS Milwaukee, 2005–06 to 2016–17, six connectedness dimensions, loneliness β=1.76 and aOR=2.14, the null for social isolation, and the family-support indirect (aOR 0.538) and direct (aOR 0.301) effects on depression are all reported correctly.

**Issue A. Headline generalizes beyond the study population** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "It is loneliness, not how often you see people, that predicts depression"
- **Abstract says:** "We analyzed longitudinal data... among Black Americans (N = 592) in the Midlife in the United States (MIDUS), Milwaukee, WI."
- **Problem:** The headline reads as a general statement about loneliness and depression. The finding comes from a single-city sample of 592 midlife Black Americans, a point the Why it matters line makes ("For midlife Black Americans at least") but the headline does not.
- **Suggested fix:** "Among midlife Black Americans, loneliness — not how often you see people — predicts depression"

---

### Study 9: Health records suggest one in six new mothers has depression-related care
**PMID:** 42745087 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

The cohort (164,767 mothers, Milan, 2017–2023), 16.0%, 23.6% with EPDS ≥8 among screened mothers, OR 8.1 for prior psychological distress, and the "modest protective" reading of lower education and employment are all accurate, as is the 10–15% conventional figure.

**Issue A. Risk factors listed as if in descending order of magnitude** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "followed by age over 40, migrant background, being unmarried and first-time motherhood"
- **Abstract says:** "age > 40 years (OR 1.3; 95% CI 1.2-1.4), migrant background (OR 1.1; 95% CI 1.1-1.2) and primiparity (OR 1.4; 95% CI 1.4-1.5)"
- **Problem:** "Followed by" implies rank order, but primiparity (1.4) is the largest of the three after prior distress and is listed last, while migrant background (1.1) is the weakest and is listed second. No OR is given for unmarried status in the abstract at all.
- **Suggested fix:** "followed at much lower magnitude by first-time motherhood (OR 1.4), age over 40 (1.3) and migrant background (1.1); unmarried status was also named as a risk factor, without a reported odds ratio."

**Issue B. Algorithm validation and EPDS "cross-check" go beyond the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "cross-checked against Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale screening" / "cases defined by an unvalidated utilization algorithm"
- **Abstract says:** "Events attributable to perinatal depression were identified through an algorithm applied to Health Care Utilization (HCU) data... Among screened mothers, 23.6% met criteria for high psychological vulnerability (EPDS ≥ 8)."
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only. The abstract reports the two figures side by side; it does not describe validating the algorithm against EPDS, nor does it state that the algorithm is unvalidated. The Caveat asserts a limitation that may or may not be true.
- **Suggested fix:** Body: "and separately reported Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale results for the screened subgroup." Caveat: "The abstract does not report validation of the utilization algorithm, so the 16% mixes true incidence with care-seeking."

---

### Study 10: Forgiveness goes with worse, not better, post-traumatic symptoms
**PMID:** 42664566 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. N=1794, the enriched population-based sample, the network-analysis design, the three consistently protective items (hope, directly facing fears, meaningful activities) and the positive forgiveness–PTSD association all match the abstract. "Goes with" is correctly non-causal for cross-sectional network data, the Why it matters line does not overreach, and the substantial Mount Sinai patent and licensing disclosures (Janssen, Click Therapeutics) are carried into both the pitch angle and Caveats.

---

### Study 11: Women in ongoing depression treatment conceive less often during fertility care
**PMID:** 42735740 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

The source population (601,664), analytic cohort (8734 controls vs 4367 with depression), all three subdistribution hazard ratios (1.10, 0.53, 0.31), the prescription-coverage finding and the authors' explicit warning against an adherence reading are reproduced accurately. The framing is appropriately restrained and the "do not imply any prescribing action" instruction is the right call.

**Issue A. A second reported outcome is omitted** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**The study:** ...Among treated women, greater prescription coverage went with a higher hazard of pregnancy — a finding the authors explicitly say should not be read as adherence improving fertility."
- **Abstract says:** "Antidepressant-treated pregnancy cohorts had higher odds of spontaneous abortion than non-depressed controls."
- **Problem:** The digest's Why it matters line argues that "recovered depression looks unremarkable for conception." The miscarriage result is a second reproductive outcome in the same abstract that a reader — or a reporting clinician — would consider material, and leaving it out makes the picture look tidier than it is.
- **Suggested fix:** Add to The study: "Antidepressant-treated cohorts who did become pregnant also had higher odds of spontaneous abortion than non-depressed controls — subject to the same confounding caveats."

---

### Study 12: People whose brains respond least to reward gain most from a single mood-training session
**PMID:** 42700813 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=92 (47/45), mean age 19.44, the MID task with EEG-recorded RewP, the null group difference in RewP, the crossover moderation pattern for perceived stress and the n=66 follow-up are all accurate, and the Caveats correctly identify this as a moderation finding on a null primary effect.

**Issue A. Headline names the wrong outcome** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "People whose brains respond least to reward gain most from a single mood-training session"
- **Abstract says:** "RewP moderated the training effects on one-month follow-up perceived stress, but not symptoms of depression or social anxiety."
- **Problem:** In a depression-focused digest for a psychology section, "gain most" invites the reader to assume mood or symptom benefit. The only moderated outcome was perceived stress; depression and social anxiety symptoms showed nothing. The body text says so, but the headline is what carries into a pitch.
- **Suggested fix:** "People whose brains respond least to reward show the biggest drop in stress after a single training session"

**Issue B. "No effects on" conflates a null main effect with a null moderation** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "There were no effects on depression or social anxiety symptoms."
- **Abstract says:** "RewP moderated the training effects on one-month follow-up perceived stress, but not symptoms of depression or social anxiety."
- **Problem:** What the abstract reports is that RewP did *not moderate* effects on depression or social anxiety; it does not separately report main effects of the training on those symptoms. The two are different claims.
- **Suggested fix:** "RewP did not moderate outcomes for depression or social anxiety symptoms."

---

### Study 13: How harshly stroke patients treat themselves in week one tracks their depression
**PMID:** 42731412 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=407, assessment within the first week post-stroke, SCS-D-KF and PHQ-9, the two-factor structure, ΔR²=0.057 for UCS versus 0.013 for CS, the hierarchical latent SEM with sociodemographic and clinical covariates, the one-third post-stroke depression figure, and the ω=0.63 reliability caveat are all correct.

- **Suggested fix:** Confirm scoring direction with the authors; until then, "uncompassionate self-responding explained the most additional variance in depressive symptoms (ΔR²=0.057)".

**Issue B. "Single-center" not stated in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Caveats: Cross-sectional...; single-center"
- **Abstract says:** "This cross-sectional study examined 407 patients (60.4% male) with acute stroke." Author affiliations span Düsseldorf, Bielefeld and University Hospital Heidelberg (Department of Neurology).

### Study 16: Refugees keep their therapy gains even when asylum decisions change
**PMID:** 42703887 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=90 with T2=59, two German psychosocial centres, self-report PTSD and depression measures, linear mixed models showing significant improvement, and the null moderation by asylum status change are all accurate. - **As written:** "Refugees keep their therapy gains even when asylum decisions change"
- **Abstract says:** "The results further cautiously hint towards the robustness of therapeutic gains across challenging legal circumstances."

### Study 17: Depression's link to advanced heart, kidney and metabolic disease is stronger in women
**PMID:** 42747918 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

NHANES, N=30,244, 16% advanced CKM, 8% with depressive symptoms, the sex-stratified ORs (women 2.24, men 1.75), the significant sex interaction and the weaker association at ≥65 versus 30–49 (OR 0.42) are all correctly reported, as is the cross-sectional caveat.

**Issue A. Two separate interactions combined into a claim about one subgroup** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "It suggests the mind–body link in cardiometabolic disease is concentrated in younger and middle-aged women — a group whose cardiovascular risk is routinely underestimated."
- **Abstract says:** "Interaction estimates indicated a stronger association among women (OR, 1.58; 95% CI, 1.12-2.23; P=0.010) and a weaker association at age ≥65 versus 30-49 years (OR, 0.42; 95% CI, 0.27-0.67; P<.001)."
- **Problem:** These are two independent effect-modification tests. The abstract reports no sex-by-age joint analysis, so there is no evidence that the association is specifically *concentrated* in younger women — that would require a three-way interaction or an age-stratified, sex-stratified estimate that the abstract does not contain. The pitch angle then builds its opening scene ("a 40-year-old woman") on this unsupported combination.
- **Suggested fix:** "It suggests the mind–body link in cardiometabolic disease is stronger in women, and — separately — stronger in younger and middle-aged adults than in the over-65s."

### Study 18: Chronic pelvic pain leaves a distinct mark on body image
**PMID:** 42600312 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

22 studies, N=7609, g=0.50 (95% CI 0.30–0.69), the comparison with healthy controls, the psychosocial correlates (anxiety, depression, loneliness, sexual dysfunction, distress) and the inclusion of vulvodynia alongside endometriosis are all accurate, and the Caveats correctly note the cross-sectional and theory-poor input literature.

**Issue A. "Mediator" is stronger than what the authors claim** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "The authors identify 'body functionality' — what the body can do rather than how it looks — as a possible mediator between pain symptoms and body image, and a candidate intervention target."
- **Abstract says:** "Body functionality may be a key outcome to consider in the relationship between condition-specific symptoms (e.g., pain) and body image concerns, demonstrating potential as a target of intervention."
- **Problem:** "Mediator" is a specific statistical claim implying a tested causal pathway. The authors say only that it may be a key outcome to consider in that relationship, and describe it as an under-researched construct needing better measurement.
- **Suggested fix:** "The authors flag 'body functionality' — what the body can do rather than how it looks — as a construct worth measuring in the relationship between pain and body image, and a candidate intervention target."

**Issue B. Headline implies a causal direction the pooled studies cannot establish** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Chronic pelvic pain leaves a distinct mark on body image"
- **Abstract says:** "Compared to healthy control groups, the meta-analysis revealed those with CPP had significantly worse body image concerns... The quality of many included studies was limited by their cross-sectional design."
- **Problem:** "Leaves a mark" describes an effect produced by the condition over time; the pooled evidence is a cross-sectional between-group difference of moderate size.
- **Suggested fix:** "Chronic pelvic pain comes with distinctly worse body image"

- **Abstract says:** "lumateperone 42 mg (a simultaneous modulator of serotonin, dopamine, and glutamate)" — described only as an approved-dose agent in a Phase 3 long-term safety study; the abstract makes no novelty claim.
